comment.value:
The paper examines the challenges of efficiently integrating $k$ monitors. Using all the available monitors would increase the quality, but it would also require additional memory and time.  Better policies are possible, especially if ones tolerate stochastic policies.

The problem is cast as a Neyman-Pearson classification, as monitors tend to have more false-positive errors. The submission demonstrated the technique using LLM for code generation. That’s both surprising and expected. Surprising because they could have used any other ML models, but it’s expected, as AI safety is particularly relevant when using LLMs.

The discussion was effective, leading to two reviewers increasing their ratings. As a result, all four reviewers rate the submission as borderline accept.

There is consensus on the quality of the technical work and the honesty of the contributions. The authors made it clear that their work supports up to a few monitors and requires a non-insignificant amount of data for calibrating the classifiers. The analysis of the regions is insightful.

Presenting it as a POMDP was not received well by a reviewer. I agree that this is not a general POMDP, but it’s a way to formally express the problem. It might be possible to use a probabilistic graphical model.

Personally, I find the story clear and that limitations can be studied in follow-up work.

Despite the consensus of borderline accept, I recommend acceptance.

author_final_remarks.value:
In our paper, we study an important and timely problem: How to combine multiple runtime AI monitors with different cost and performance profiles. Monitor protocols with multiple monitors are already used today in production environments, such as ChatGPT Agent. However, existing protocols and academic work do not use principled methods to combine these monitors, relying instead on heuristics. In our paper, we outline a rigorous mathematical framework for constructing monitor protocols and demonstrate empirically that they can lead to safety gains. Reviewers noted that the paper is well-written and clearly explained our core ideas.

We thank the reviewers for their helpful comments. While many reviewers were concerned about the significance of our work, recent news of companies using multiple monitors has affirmed that studying how to construct monitoring protocols is an impactful and important research area. Reviewers were also rightly concerned about issues from distribution shift. If we fit our thresholds to a specific training distribution, these thresholds could be suboptimal in deployment. However, we argue that the right metric is not whether the thresholds are perfectly optimal, but whether they are better than not using empirical data at all. In our additional experiment on an OOD dataset, we showed that our optimized monitor protocol still significantly outperforms naive baselines.

We believe our paper makes a well-scoped contribution to the growing literature on monitoring AIs. We are grateful for the constructive feedback, which has allowed us to strengthen the paper and resolve key initial concerns. Our work provides a practical, data-driven alternative to the ad-hoc methods currently used in industry, and we hope the committee will recognize its value for building safer, more reliable AI systems.

rebuttal.value:
We thank reviewers for their comments. We’ll first give a general overview of the paper’s strengths and answer some common objections. Then dive into answering specific questions. 

## Significance of our work

Our paper is focused on optimally combining information from runtime monitors with different cost and performance profiles. We study how to rigorously construct these protocols agnostic to the specific setting. This is an increasingly important problem in AI safety. Since the Neurips submission deadline, OpenAI has announced that they use a combination of two monitors for ChatGPT Agent’s bio-misuse mitigation, and Anthropic researchers put out a new paper on using multiple probe-based monitors with varied costs. However, neither paper presents a principled way of combining monitors: 

Cunningham et al.’s “Cost-Effective Constitutional Classifiers via Representation Re-use” tests various probe-based monitors with different overhead computational costs. They combine monitors using the simple heuristic of “use the cheap monitor first, and if suspicious, use the expensive monitor. ” Instead of finding the optimal region to call the second monitor at a set of budgets to sketch out the cost curve, they simply sweep over the threshold on when to call the second monitor to vary spend (Figure 4). Instead of using likelihood ratios to combine the two monitors when two are called, they only use data from the second monitor. 

OpenAI’s “ChatGPT Agent System Card” section 5.2.2.2. also mentions the use of a monitoring system consisting of two monitors. Their first monitor checks if the content is related to biology. If so, a second monitor checks whether the response or prompt contains hazardous information. This shows that monitoring protocols constructed from multiple monitors are already used in production AI systems for AI safety.

To be clear, it’s possible that our optimized algorithm will also recommend a final strategy of “use cheap monitor first, then use expensive monitor, and only rely on expensive monitor’s scores if they’re available.” It’s also possible that practitioners have some strong prior over which monitors are more robust and trustworthy, and choose a simpler or regularized strategy in lieu of something fitted to the data like the one we proposed. However, we believe it’s important to showcase how to construct these protocols in a rigorous, data-driven manner. 

The existing literature also relies on heuristics to construct these protocols. McKenzie et al.’s “Detecting High-Stakes Interactions with Activation Probes” chooses when to call the second monitor based on how close the first monitor’s score is to the median (as a heuristic measure for uncertainty). Parrack et al.’s “Benchmarking Deception Probes via Black-to-White Performance Boosts” and McKenzie et al. both take a simple weighted average of multiple monitors to make the final auditing decision, as opposed to using likelihood ratio methods. We hope reviewers will reconsider the timeliness and importance of our work given these new papers, and we will incorporate these citations into our paper. 

## New experiment addressing OOD shift and diverse settings

Reviewers also brought up the lack of diverse settings in our experiments, how our “malicious” code from o1-mini is not sufficiently obscured, and how distributional shifts could reduce the performance of the protocol. We do think distributional shift could be a serious issue: if we overfit to training data, we might do worse on real-world deployments. However, the right comparison is “Are we doing better than not fitting at all?” We ran an additional experiment where we took the thresholds fit to the o1-mini generated backdoors on BigCodeBench, and tested the monitoring protocol’s performance on a random sample of backdoored code from Wen et al. “Adaptive Deployment of Untrusted LLMs Reduces Distributed Threats.” These are backdoored code generated using a much more optimized pipeline on the APPS dataset, which acts as a good out-of-distribution test. 

While the overall safety scores decrease significantly, we find that the order in which policies do the best remains the same across all experiments. For the main result in Figure six, when the total budget is 1.5, $\Pi_\text{SR}$’s safety decreased from 82% to 48% on the OOD set, but it still outperforms always using both monitors (24%), or using only the 70B model (32% safety) or 8B model (39% safety). The results are also similar in single monitor settings, where $\Pi_\text{NPS}$ outperforms $\Pi_\text{NP}$, which outperforms $\Pi_\text{Naive}$. Thus, for this specific distribution shift, it was better that we had fitted our thresholds to the data. Future work could test distribution shifts that are more likely to occur for specific settings that we’re constructing monitoring protocols for. At runtime, practitioners could also continue to incorporate new data into the training set and tune the thresholds to keep them updated.

Generally, we think the strength of our paper lies in our principled and rigorous theoretical framework. The important comparison is “Does our paper provide a better way of combining monitors compared to heuristic baselines?” Given that most policy classes search over options which include the heuristic baselines (such as “call the cheap monitor first and the expensive monitor if it’s above a certain threshold”), we think the answer is trivially yes.

## Adding a new guide on how to apply our methods

Finally, reviewer f693 and RTmL have found our work cleanly written (thank you!). Our goal is to provide an easy-to-follow guide to real-world practitioners building monitoring protocols. Given the rise in systems combining probe-based monitors and black box monitors, we added a guide that walks through an example on how to combine probe monitors and black box monitors using data from Parrack et al., making our work even more approachable.

## Additional responses for reviewer RTmL

**Re distribution shift**: See above. 

**Re scalability issues & how common our setup is**: We do not explore cases with more than four monitors because we think they are well served by existing literature on costly classification trees or costly classification RL (see lines 70-74 and 293-296). Again, existing monitoring systems are mostly using two monitors and clumsily combining them, and thus we think this paper addresses an important and timely problem. Systems using two monitors are already used for ChatGPT Agent, and we think they’ll only become more commonplace in the future.

summary.value: This paper develops a formal framework and practical protocol for optimally combining multiple AI runtime monitors under a unified cost constraint, using likelihood-ratio-based decision policies and exhaustive search to maximize recall for detecting misaligned model outputs while respecting budget limits; the approach is validated on code backdoor detection using Llama 3.1 70B/8B monitors and demonstrates strong empirical improvements over baseline strategies.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

+ this paper introduces , general method for cost-sensitive composition of multiple runtime monitors using rigorous likelihood ratio theory.

+ this paper provides a thorough empirical analysis and ablations showing that combining monitors yields superior safety-recall trade-offs compared to single-monitor or naïve approaches.

Weakness: 

+ The scalability of the proposed method is limited, as exhaustive policy search is only tractable for a small number of monitors and simple invocation strategies.

+ The method’s robustness under severe distribution shift or with more diverse/complex monitors is not fully evaluated.

+ Qualitative failure cases and breakdowns for different attack types are limited; more analysis would increase transparency.

summary.value: This paper considers the budgeting problem of when to call a more expensive monitor when trying to detect AI misalignment. This paper proposes approach for determining this threshold based on some training data and a fixed budget. The proposed approach is empirically evaluated on a single task of detecting whether or not an AI system has output code with a backdoor or not. The authors show that there approach provides a Pareto improvement over just using a single monitor.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### Strengths
* The paper presents a simple and easy-to-understand budgeting strategy for choosing when to call an additional more expensive monitor.
* The result of the dip in log-likelihood where higher monitor scores do not necessarily correspond to higher precision (Figure 2a) is very interesting.
* The results on this limited setup are fairly good and shows the benefit of this approach in a limited toy setting.

### Weaknesses
* The paper is not well motivated in the text. The paper somewhat assumes that the reader is familiar with prior AI control and monitoring work, and it just assumes that the importance of this problem is self-evident. Monitoring is obviously important for AI safety, but why is this problem important in particular? The text does not answer this question adequately. (I believe this problem is important - this is more about the writing.)
* The experiments are quite limited. The approach is evaluated in one scenario on one dataset, with only two external monitors. Section 4 just shows that the large expensive monitor works fairly well at detecting backdoors in code (not even that great though). Section 6 shows how to trade-off two monitors.
* A massive limitation acknowledged by the authors is that the learned threshold might not generalize to out-of-distribution data, but they make no effort to try this on more than one scenario.
* The toy scenario is somewhat fabricated especially since o1 is not being told to obfuscate the backdoors it is creating. This is a very weak simulation of deception.
* The proposed approach is made to seem much more profound and complicated than it is in actuality. For example, the authors refer to a learned threshold for choosing whether or not to call an additional more powerful monitor, and depending on the results, which outputs should be audited (essentially the most powerful monitor) a policy. They also describe this general enumeration of all possible monitor combinations, which they do not even do themselves in their experiments. Calling the choice of which monitors to call a POMDP is quite the stretch.
* Furthermore, the final approach is not so sophisticated and seems like the first thing someone would try when given this problem: just learn a threshold for when the next most expensive monitor (auditing is just a very expensive and very accurate monitor) should be called based on some training data.

questions.value:
* Why is there just a fixed budget and how would we know what this is in practice?
* Adding Gaussian noise to the monitor scores seems like a terrible way to make them continuous. The more reasonable way to do this is to extract the logits for each of the digits from the output layer of the Llama model (either 8B or 70B) and compute a weighted expectation from that categorical distribution (over the tokens "0", "1", ..., "9") by applying softmax to the logits. 
* Why is this an important problem that warrants an entire paper about it?

summary.value:
This paper addresses the challenge of optimising safety interventions in AI systems under cost constraints by combining runtime monitors. The authors formulate the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where the goal is to learn a policy that decides when and which monitors to invoke, and when to audit outputs based on monitor scores, in order to maximise recall on misaligned outputs while respecting a fixed budget.

They evaluate their framework on BigCodeBench, focusing on detecting backdoored code samples. Results show that a stochastic monitoring policy, which may audit without always querying a monitor, achieves higher recall under the same cost compared to deterministic baselines that always call monitors. Furthermore, they demonstrate that a stochastic combination of two monitors can strictly outperform all single-monitor policies, including those that always invoke both monitors.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Pros:
=====
* The paper introduces a mathematical formulation (as a POMDP) for combining runtime monitors under budget constraints.
* It also shows that smart combinations of monitors can achieve higher recall at the same or lower cost.
* The evaluation is done on a realistic setting: backdoor detection in AI-generated code (BigCodeBench).
* The paper is generally well-written. There are small typos in places, e.g. use of \PI_{TM} in Figure 5, but \PI_{BM} in the text describing it.

Cons:
=====
* The paper's method relies on the distribution of misaligned examples being stable. This comes from the training data and is assumed to reflect the real-world distribution the system will face during deployment. However, in practice distributions shift, which may negatively impact the audit decisions.
* Finding the optimal monitoring protocol requires enumerating all possible monitor calling strategies. This brute force search is intractable beyond 4 monitors, and the paper doesn't explore any approximate or scalable learning method.

Both my concerns are acknowledged by the authors under limitations. However, I'm not sure if this makes it better. They are still pretty serious limitations that make me doubt the practical applicability of the proposed technique.

final_justification.value: During the discussion period, the authors made a case for the practical applicability of their work despite scalability issues. I appreciate their perspective and therefore maintain my positive assessment. However, the cons in my initial review remain. In particular, regarding the authors' OOD experiment, it is unclear how representative it is of real-world misalignment. The drop in safety score from 82% to 48% is substantial, raising concerns about the method’s absolute effectiveness under realistic distribution shifts. Also. although I appreciate the authors' explanation of the practical utility of two monitors, the technique's scalability limitations persist.

title.value: Combining Cost Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety

TLDR.value: Optimally constructing monitoring protocols with multiple monitors of varying costs and performances.

abstract.value: Monitoring AIs at runtime can help us detect and stop harmful actions. In this paper, we study how to efficiently combine multiple runtime monitors into a single monitoring protocol. The protocol's objective is to maximize the probability of applying a safety intervention on misaligned outputs (i.e., maximize recall). Since running monitors and applying safety interventions are costly, the protocol also needs to adhere to an average-case budget constraint. Taking the monitors' performance and cost as given, we develop an algorithm to find the best protocol. The algorithm exhaustively searches over when and which monitors to call, and allocates safety interventions based on the Neyman-Pearson lemma. By focusing on likelihood ratios and strategically trading off spending on monitors against spending on interventions, we more than double our recall rate compared to a naive baseline in a code review setting. We also show that combining two monitors can Pareto dominate using either monitor alone. Our framework provides a principled methodology for combining existing monitors to detect undesirable behavior in cost-sensitive settings.
